title: Think Differently Special Edition Increasing the Urgency on Acquisition Speed and Security 11.9.21

cues.text: >> Like to welcome everybody to today's DAU event.
Time's another episode of the Think Differently series.
This is Increasing the Urgency of Acquisition Speed and Security.
My name is Emmett Simmons, I'm the producer for today's event.
We also have Dr. Marina Theodotou on as our moderator.
Couple of quick items.
The microphones will be muted.
The session is being recorded and will be posted to DAU.edu/DAU-webcasts.
We are taking questions today.
Please submit your questions via the chat.
We will be responding to questions verbally towards the end of the event.
There is a survey, we will be posting the survey link in the chat.
If you're here for CLPs, the session does qualify for up
to 1.5 CLPs with supervisor approval.
It is not automatic, you will need to apply for it.
But there will be a CLP certificate at the end of the survey,
where you can copy and paste the link to get it.
And now I'm going to turn it over to Dr. Marina Theodotou to introduce our speakers.
>> Thank you so much, Emmett.
It's wonderful to be here today.
Welcome everyone for this special edition of Think Differently.
We're super excited to have an amazing panel with us today.
And we'll go ahead and introduce each one of our sparks, starting with Mr. David Rader,
who is a deputy director in the Office
of Foreign Investment Review at the Department of Defense.
And his portfolio focus is on national economic security, foreign direct investment,
trade policy, and matters under the purview of the Committee
on Foreign Investment in the United States.
You probably know it as CFIUS.
David holds a BA in political science, MA in government,
JD in corporate bankruptcy law, and an MS in finance.
He's a team member of the Council of Foreign Relations.
David, welcome, and thank you for joining us today.
>> Thanks.
Great to be here.
>> Next, we're delighted to welcome Mr. Scott Tait, who's the executive director
of the National Security Innovation Catalyst at the University of California San Diego.
He previously served 27 years as an officer in the US Navy,
where he held senior policy positions with a focus in Indo-Asia, on the joint chiefs
of staff, J-5, Pacific fleet staff, and US Seventh Fleet staff.
Scott, welcome.
We're delighted to have you with us.
>> Thank you, Marina.
It's a pleasure to be here.
>> Next, we're delighted to welcome Dr. Rebecca Keiser, who is the chief research--
chief of research security, strategy, and policy at the National Science Foundation.
Dr. Keiser is the first chief of research security, strategy, and policy,
a position established in March of 2020 to ensure the security
of federally funded research while maintaining open international collaboration.
In this role, Dr. Keiser provides the NSF director with policy advice
on all aspects of research security strategy.
She also leads NSF's efforts to develop and implement efforts to improve research security,
and the agency's coordination with other federal agencies at the White House.
Dr. Keiser, welcome.
>> Thank you, it's a pleasure to be here.
>> Alright.
Next. We'd like to welcome Mr. Jay Young, who's a senior advisor with the Office
of Commercial and Economic Analysis, OCEA.
Strategic initiatives at the US Air Force.
Mr. Young has had a long career in industry, which has included senior positions
in strategy planning and marketing and sales in several industries,
including diversified manufacturing, information technology services, and management consulting.
He's also a retired Naval Reserve Captain, who during his 25 year career,
commanded two reserve intelligence units and served with Indo-Pacific Command,
Southern Command, and US Seventh Fleet,
as well as supporting the Office of the Secretary of Defense.
Jay, welcome.
We're delighted to have you with us today.
>> Thank you, Marina.
Very happy to be here.
Looking forward to it.
>> Next, we'd love to welcome Dr. David Gallop, one of DAU's own,
who is also leading the [inaudible] group discussing today.
Dr. Gallop is the director for the DAU Leadership Center.
In that role, he's charged with delivering leadership learning
and development opportunities to all levels of the Acquisition Workforce.
He places special emphasis on the civilian members of the workforce.
Welcome, David, it's great to have you here.
>> Thank you, Marina, it's great to be here.
>> And last but not least, Professor Steve Blasch, who is also a PUMP and the lead
of the initial study we'll be discussing today.
Dr. Blasch has joined the DAU team in 2017 after completing 23 year career
in the United States Navy and four years as a DoD contractor.
He's an extractor for six modules at DAU of RQM 3100 and the course manager
for RQM 4030, Requirements Executive Overview.
And he's the Navy customer liaison on the DAU team responsible for the development
of capability requirements workforce.
In this role, he works closely with joint staff, OSD, services, and the agencies to comply
with Section 801 of the fiscal year 2007 National Defense Authorization Act.
And holds a Level C in requirements management certification training.
Steve, welcome.
We're delighted that you were able to join us today as well.
>> Thank you, looking forward to it.
>> So, with that, let's get started.
We have a great conversation prepared for you today.
And what we wanted to do is give you a couple of pieces
of information as backdrop to our discussion.
First of all, as your host and curator of this Think Differently episode, we're super excited
to highlight that this is a special edition,
because typically it's just me and Emmett producing this.
But now we have a whole team behind this.
Both in thinking and generating the ideas behind our discussion today, but also supporting.
So I'd like to thank our DAU services, video services team, as well as a whole host
of DAU faculty and staff over in 19 that are part
of this initiative we'll be discussing today.
So, when we think about Great Power Competition and we think about acquisition,
it is critical to highlight that speed and security are paramount.
To address this challenge, DAU is leading an effort to increase the sense of urgency
across the national security ecosystem, industry, and academia.
By embracing a set of principles to change the way the acquisition workforce thinks, learns,
and leads in terms of acquisition programs and outcomes.
Today's discussion brings together different perspectives to discuss Great Power Competition,
and what really this means when it comes to speed and security.
So we're going to go ahead and get started.
And with that, my first question is for Jay.
Jay, you have spent a lot of time at OCEA, along with your time,
analyzing Great Power Competition and understanding what this challenge means.
Secretary Austin said that China is a pacing challenge.
And your team has done a lot of work to try to understand what this threat means.
And what we'd like for you to help us do is help us understand what is the nature of the threat?
>> Thank you, Marina.
Will do. Office of Commercial and Economic Analysis of which I am a part has been working
to understand the scope and scale of what China's engaged
in from an economic standpoint, in particular, for some years.
And let me just be very clear about what it is that China's strategic goal here.
They are engaged in an effort - largely state-driven, developmental effort -
to ensure that China emerges as the leader in those industries and technologies
that will form the foundation of national power in the 21st century.
Let me just stress, they're not trying to catch up,
they're not trying to, you know, just close a gap.
What they're trying to do, and they believe that this is the time to do it,
is to become the leaders in these areas that they have targeted for advancement.
And there's three key components to this that I'll just touch on briefly.
First and foremost, there is a national industrial strategy.
Known by the umbrella term of innovation development driven strategy,
of which the critical part is called Made in China 2025.
And within Made in China 2025, they have identified 10 areas of focus
that China believes are the areas of technology in the industries where they want to be superior
and have devoted resources at a substantial scale to those.
And they range from everything from advanced manufacturing to various types
of green technologies, to artificial intelligence and quantum computing,
[inaudible] of information technology.
It's a set of those technologies that would not surprise anyone that understands
where these emerging areas of the economy and the technology are going.
So China has been very clear about this, they have devoted a vast amount of resources
to ensuring that they can envelope these capabilities.
Their latest five year plan, the 14th five year plan, reinforces this discipline and this focus.
And if anything, increases the urgency.
There's a stronger sense of urgency about the need for China to achieve faster a level
of self sufficiency in many of these areas that they've targeted.
One notable one is semiconductors.
There's two other elements of this broad national program
that I'll mention here as backdrop.
One is the one which I think many people have heard of, the Belt and Road Initiative.
Or One Belt, One Road.
This is a massive international development program which X-intercept Jinping has put
as the centerpiece of China's foreign policy.
It is really focused on the development of global infrastructure
in transportation logistics, both from a physical and logical standpoint.
There's a heavy IT telecommunications component known
as the digital silk road that's a part of this.
But it's operational on 140 countries are part of it, and it's operating
on almost every continent at some level.
And again, the purpose here is for China to ultimately construct a trading system
in which Chinese industries, Chinese standards, Chinese technologies are really the centerpiece
with China at the middle of this altered global trading system.
So again, an ambitious vision, which they are putting substantial resources behind.
And finally, there is a program called military civil fusion.
Which again, I'm sure some people have heard of.
Which is really an effort by China to ensure that its military forces
and their R&D capabilities are fused very carefully with those elements
of the civilian economy that are engaged in these leading technology areas, so the benefits,
the advancements that occur in the civilian economy are translated as rapidly
as possible to the military side of things.
And we've seen, you know, evidence in how quickly China can deploy a large
and modern military, the nature and scope of the military buildup that they have undertaken
over the course of the last 20 years.
The latest China military report put up by DoD stresses that.
So again, it's the nature of this effort, the scope and scale,
the level of resources they're putting behind it.
There's evidence in a number of industries where they've been successful in beginning
to dominate the entire value chain of critical industries.
The maritime one is a good example.
They've targeted everything from aquaculture to ship leasing,
and now have a very strong maritime capability across that value chain that includes shipyards,
maintenance, repair, as well as other elements of that entire value chain.
So again, it's a holistic strategy engaged at a national level, fusing the capabilities
of both the public and the private sector.
China believes that this government directed market economy, as they call it,
gives them very specific advantages in the 21st century that will enable them
to achieve these longer-term strategic goals.
So those are really the foundational pieces of this, Marina.
I'll stop there and turn it back over to you.
But hopefully that provides some backdrop for what China's doing, the scope and scale
of the ambition, and the urgency, quite frankly, that they see as being necessary in order
to achieve these very ambitious goals.
>> Thank you, Jay, for setting the stage for this conversation and providing us the backdrop
for what the Secretary Austin has called China
at the pacing threat, or pacing challenge, rather.
So with that, I wanted to turn it over to David Rader to get--
David, we'd like to get your perspective.
Your role as deputy director in the Office of Foreign Investment Review,
you're focusing on reviewing the veracity of foreign direct investments in the United States.
So, how does the Great Power Competition element come into play to your efforts?
>> Yeah. First like to thank you for inviting me and DAU for hosting this great event.
I pride myself on being an original thinker, but Jay absolutely nailed it.
Couldn't agree more with all your comments about framing the problem, both as COCs and OSD.
So my office is a represented [inaudible],
the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States.
It's an interagency body.
But we have our own capabilities and authorities in which we operate.
And so, a few things about kind of like what we're doing is we're really, I would say,
to get a better understanding of the power of competition, China specific,
integrating a lot of commercial tools and capabilities.
We're increasing our workforce from a skill standpoint.
That's not a shot at anybody, but it's such a complex domain
that you can't just have policy folks, you can't just have lawyers,
you can't just have intel officers, you know, or economists.
It has to all be married together, because it's kind of Rubik's cube of how technology,
the economy, and all these different factors come together is critical.
Because if you look at it as in the vertical, you're going to miss the big picture.
So those commercial tools, we're working very hard, we're doing a lot of engagement.
Like me here today, getting out west, getting out to Europe,
getting to our partners around the world, if you will.
Allies and partners both on the commercial side and the government side, to figure out kind
of what they ecosystems look like.
And so to Jay's point, that kind of top-down Made in China 2025.
What is China looking at?
What do they want?
And it goes beyond China.
And so kind of understanding who is coming up, who's in stealth mode,
which industries are emerging, which agencies are trying to figure out what does this mean?
What does AI do?
And so, looking at that through our relationships, our commercial tools,
and then the experts and experience from pulling in.
And then also, you know, the President and White House and Secretary have done a great job
of identifying the criticality of supply chains.
I have a frustration, because that's a word that's used vaguely.
It's a little overused.
But I think we're starting to have a very good understanding of how to narrowly map them out.
How to find choke points, criticality, you know, failure points,
as well as ways to accentuate the areas we need to grow.
So I think my last comment about kind of what the Department's doing, what my office is doing,
what the Committee is doing, is also looking to understand--
better understand financial tools and instruments.
You know, [inaudible] ownership, complex debt structures, you know,
a lot of previous minds it was well they would just show
up with a bag of cash and buy the company.
And it's not that simple anymore.
Between cryptocurrency, and complex debt structures, like I said, and family offices,
and things we're wrapping our hands around and head around,
a lot of emphasis is being placed on that.
So we can map out how the global economy moves from a macro sense all the way
down to those microinvestments, and then you crosswalk that or layer it
in in a matrix style, with that emerging tack.
And China's objectives and our own national priorities.
So it's a big problem set.
We're pulling in lots more people, a lot of commercial relationships,
including our friends at OCEA who do a great job, too.
And really leaning on each other.
And I'm going to use the statement, hold the government, hold the country approach.
But that's in the forefront of our mind now in how we look
to incentivize foreign direct investment, but also protect what's important to us.
So pause there and turn it back to you.
>> Thanks so much, David.
So you've talked about this being-- both you and Jay talked
about this pacing challenge being both complex and-- all encompassing.
All across the different sectors of the economy, people, process, technology, governance, data.
And now I'd like to turn it over to Dr. Keiser, Rebecca, to talk about the research side.
So there is the academic side that is also affected by Great Power Competition.
And in particular, the Chinese challenge.
Rebecca, what is your organization doing
and how is the National Science Foundation addressing this challenge?
Over to you.
>> Thank you.
Well, first let me say that of course the United States continues
to welcome international talent.
And international research talent into the United States.
We value it.
It has made us a great country.
And we need to continue that.
However, we are concerned that the government of China is exploiting our open research system
in unethical and sometimes illegal ways for its own benefit.
As Jay said, the plan of the Chinese government to succeed in science technology is very clear.
Fundamental, basic research is a big part of that as well.
And there are huge investments being made in everything from astronomy to ocean research.
Something that the Chinese government has realized is that it needs talent.
It needs talent to come back to China in order
to transfer the knowledge needed for the scientific advances.
Unfortunately, that has caused the government of China
to exploit our open research system in several ways.
And one of the main ways is through foreign government talent recruitment programs.
And these are programs that the Chinese government has instituted
at many different levels, from the national level to the provincial level.
And it is a form of recruiting US researchers to not only work for Chinese entities,
but to do so without disclosing to their US full-time employer
that they are working for these Chinese entities.
They often have a second lab in China in addition to their lab in the United States.
They often transfer knowledge, pre-publication knowledge and information,
to the Chinese government for Chinese government ownership and use.
Without it going into the open system.
And these are things, of course, that are extremely concerning to us.
What is extremely concerning as well as is
that the US federal government is providing massive amounts of research funding
to these researchers who are also not disclosing these ties to the Chinese government to us.
And so we're emphasizing many things.
First of all, we're emphasizing that we do need to maintain the openness of our research system.
It's made us great.
But second, a big part of that openness is preserving the aspects of research integrity
that we all need to do, both international partnerships and in the practice
of research here in the United States.
And that means being transparent about where one gets one's funding, about one's affiliations,
about who one is collaborating with, and making sure that you are an active
and beneficial participant in the research system.
We have to address these problems head on.
And I do have to say that many US universities are more and more aware
of these concerns of research security.
And we're dealing with this together.
And I'm happy to talk further about how we're addressing this in further discussion.
Thanks.
>> Thank you, Rebecca.
Thank you for explaining to us how critical is security when it comes to research.
And that's a great segue to Scott, who leads a center, National Security Center,
at University of California San Diego.
Scott, over to you discuss a little bit what does your center do,
and how are you addressing the Great Power Competition and Chinese pacing challenge?
>> Thank you, Marina.
So we funded the catalyst project about two years ago
to really bring together national security practitioners
from across the national security spectrum.
Because as we've heard from the excellent comments from our first three panelists,
one of the things that really characterizes this competition is--
and makes it different from our previous Great Power Competitions is this idea
that it cascades across everything.
You know, so much more nuanced and interconnected than say what we dealt
with in regard to the Soviet Union.
So we bring everybody that we can to the table across not only federal government
but local and state governments as well.
For work with technologists to figure
out exactly how we can move faster and be more secure.
But also to bring some of the lessons from what the policy school is studying.
I've had the good fortune to work with Dr. [inaudible] Min Chong [phonetic] out here
who has done some incredible research on geoeconomic Great Power Competition
between the US and China and the framework that they're using.
That Jay described.
So as we both move faster but also make sure people have a good awareness of the threat,
and we work with a lot of small companies.
And a good many of them are doing some type of defense in government contracting
and just making sure that they understand the framework that they're in.
Yeah, I would argue that the number one thing that any leader in any company
of any size today has to do is be able to provide a narrative to every single employee
that this isn't the cybersecurity problem,
it isn't a physical security problem, it's an everybody problem.
And if they don't understand this framework,
the Chinese approach is pretty clear and they're open about it.
Right? Demoralize is the first thing they do, they try to underline confidence
in the institution, sometimes in the company.
Then they come in and they destabilize by actively pitting factions
within whatever the institution is against each other, whether it's government or commercial.
Then they try to push it to some sort of conflict and failure.
And then they'll try to restabilize it or buy it or do something else.
But on their own terms.
And then people see that whole framework and understand where all
of these different district data points that any one of them on its own might not look
that threatening or might not appear to be a pattern, you know, if you can convince people
that this really is a very deliberate and intentional attack
on them and on our society as a whole.
It makes it easier for them to collaborate and to really help the institution,
the organization identify and manage these risks.
Back over to you.
>> Thanks, Scott.
So, we've heard from Jay and David and Rebecca and Scott about how complex
and overarching this approach that China is taking is critical.
And from an acquisition perspective, our focus has been on ensuring
that the workforce understand and embraces this focus on both speed and security.
So, while previously, there was a choice, we thought that we had to choose.
It's either speed or security.
But from what we've heard so far, it's so critical to not differentiate
between the two, but focus on both.
Speed and security.
And with that, DAU has initiated a grassroots conversation to address the threat and inspire
and empower the workforce to think differently and embrace the speed and security elements.
And to further introduce this initiative, I'd like to invite Dr. Gallop to--
who is the champion of the initiative at DAU, to discuss a little bit,
what is this DAU initiative, David?
And why is DAU mobilizing now?
Over to you, David.
>> Yeah. Thank you, Marina.
And thank you to all the panelists for your great insights.
It's really good to have these thoughts shared within the community.
And for folks in the audience, I'm sure you know
that DAU is the Defense Acquisition Workforce's corporate university.
And everyday I'm amazed at what the acquisition workforce can do,
including leaders at all levels of organizations.
And they've been asked to do tremendous things over the last 20 years.
But there's a portion of the workforce that was borne from the 90s and later
that only knows acquisition pretty much from a Global War on Terrorism perspective.
And the skills that some of our older, more seasoned workforce have related
to Great Power Competition, they need to be brought back to the forefront.
And it really requires a shift in mindset, going from Global War
on Terrorism to Great Power Competition.
The good news is I believe our workforce is ready to step up,
it just needs this conversation and leaders to help inculcate principles
that are easily applied within the workforce.
So DAU sits in this very interesting intersection between the policy makers
on one hand and the practitioners on the other.
And DAU's really helping to set the conditions for successful policy.
As we make this shift in mindset.
So this is a great opportunity for DAU to do what it does best, and that's connect people
of likeminded opinions to make change happen.
So, I think that's really the why of DAU at this point.
And the why now?
I could be really simple and say tomorrow might be too late.
Right? We've got to make this shift now.
Keeping in mind all the great things we've done under the conditions of the Global War
on Terrorism, but take those lessons learned and apply them in the new,
strategic Great Power Competition environment.
So that's I have to say on that point, Marina, and I'll send it back to you.
>> Thank you, David.
So it's exciting.
DAU is taking the lead in-- within the acquisition realm to bring together people
from academia and national security and industry and other agencies,
so that they can be part of this conversation.
And what I wanted to do now is turn it over to Steve to hear a little bit
about what is DAU actually doing?
How many people are on this team?
Steve, you're leading this effort on a day-to-day basis for the last 90 days.
And I'm-- as a disclaimer, I'm proud to be part of this team and actually working alongside
with several other DAU faculty to help drive this forward.
So Steve, over to you.
Can you explain to us a little bit what is this DAU initiative
and what has the team achieved so far?
And what's ahead?
>> Okay, thank you.
I will try my best to do all that.
And so for those folks that don't know, this effort actually began--
it's hard to believe, almost 90 days ago.
And we've got 19 faculty from DAU that are part of this team, including Marina and Dave.
And then we've also got up to 30 external stakeholders.
Which have contributed and helped us stay within-- and given sanity checks along the way.
So we've done it-- we've worked from small to larger scope.
So, the-- so, as mentioned before, you know, Dave mentioned before, you know,
we are at-- we are the crossroads.
And we have got those stakeholders from industry, government, academia.
And a lot of it has actually helped us craft language, more universal language
in the principles and things like that.
So, and how to reach everybody.
So, what we're really trying to do is create a sense of urgency,
like Marina was talking about, about Great Power Competition.
And then this is through the tenants of the speed and security, you know,
with respect to technological development and procurement.
So, from the beginning, you know, and as you can see, I think,
from the previous panelists, the awareness is there.
And also, and what we've discovered and confirmed along the way,
and this is from all the stakeholders as well,
is that the urgency just isn't there in some of the organizations.
And we want to, you know, really get it going.
So, what we did was these previous 90 days, we broke it in to go to an agile approach.
A term, we went to three sprints, if you will.
And the first sprint was just to create an make a very simple set
of principles that everybody could understand.
Sounds easy, it was-- took a lot of work and effort to get there.
A lot of this was done virtually and through-- and we did a small sprint within that.
And had a [inaudible] product, went out to our stakeholders and got some good input.
Then the next stage was we wanted to, now that we have that, we wanted to socialize
and finalize, you know, shape the principles a little more.
So we had a working group meeting.
And that had approximately, I think it was 17 stakeholders came in and helped us
and we got input via a virtual working group.
And then the final stage here is culminating and agreeing and also promoting these principles,
which is what we're doing here today.
It's the reason why we're here today.
This is a culminating event for this overall sprint of the 90 days.
And just to look back, that second work sprint, that working group back
in October was really critical in providing us some great input.
So we want to thank our 29 co-contributors and co-authors.
It's very important to know that we have co-authors.
And they collectively helped us shape all these principles.
So, that's what's been done.
Now looking forward on our path is we have-- we want to establish a collective vision.
You know, inspire our stakeholders to adopt, proliferate, take these back,
live by these principles, promote them.
How can-- you know, how can you take these and apply them to your organization?
Can you use them for new employee training?
Can you use them as part of writing some policy for your corporation?
You know, increase that sense of urgency.
And then we also-- so that's the collectivism to create the urgency.
And then we want to expand and continue it.
So, the objective here is to have a staining sense of urgency
that goes well beyond this initiative, this start.
We just want to light, you know, light the fire.
And we want everybody else to take it forward.
So, we're going to-- we're looking at several things.
We're looking at something like a landing page.
Where we would go and we would have the principles hosted on there.
We would have a way to exchange ideas.
We would have important links.
We would have other things that would be of interest to everybody.
And-- and then that is going to be forthcoming.
So, we look forward to everybody's help along the way.
And we really, once again, thank everybody's help to this point.
Marina, back to you.
>> Thanks so much, Steve.
So, as you were speaking, we actually posted a copy of the call to action.
It's available, the seven principles are available on the event webpage.
And we shared the link here in the chat.
So that our audience can take a look while we are talking.
And thank you so much, Steve, for sharing with us what the team has done
so far and where we're going from here.
So, essentially, the DAU team and the various other contributors
that you mentioned came together and started thinking about how do we create a conversation
and a set of principles that we can all stand behind and embrace and adopt and adapt
into our agencies and our contexts, so that we can support
and shield basically American national security and the economy?
And as I review these seven principles, I see that several of them are talking about people.
They're talking about people, they're talking about the supply chain,
we're talking about data, we're talking about ensuring that there is speed
and security in all of our processes.
And we're also talking about the principles are-- the last principle is probably my--
the one that I'll highlight, because this is the goal of what we're doing here today,
which is welcoming more likeminded people into this conversation.
And what we wanted to do now, so the first part of our conversation was to set the stage
and understand in a very short amount of time what is this--
pacing challenge that we're faced with?
And how multifaceted it is.
And also give you a sense of what DAU is doing to be part of this effort
to address the challenge and focus the acquisition workforce,
specifically on speed and security.
In this second part of our conversation, we'd like to come back to our speakers
and get their thoughts on the call to action elements and principles.
And perhaps have a more detailed discussion as to how could some
of these elements be used in their context?
And how could the various agencies broadly could embrace and come back
and be part of this conversation.
This is again a discussion, the Think Differently series focuses
on creating a platform for thought leaders to share their perspective.
This is a public event.
And these perspectives are not necessarily those of the Department of Defense in particular,
or DAU, or your agency, we are having a conversation here with our individual speakers.
So, we also have some poll questions that we will launch in a few minutes that we'd
like to get the audience to participate in this conversation and share their perspective.
So these poll questions are coming forth shortly.
And to get started on the second part of the discussion, I'd like to come back to David.
And start with you, David.
And get your perspective on this initiative, on the call to action.
And any other thoughts that you'd like to share about any
of the elements of the principles at large.
Over to you, David.
>> Yeah, yeah, thanks for that.
The seven principles look great.
I already copied Jay and said he did a good job and he saved me a lot of work.
I'm going to do the same with you in identifying that last one.
The likeminded, you know, pulling the same people in the room.
I think it's very important for those in this community to understand
in some areas, defense is an absolute leader.
